refusing information so as not to feel the obligation is willful ignorance. If someone can't bear to see what happens to the animals they eat, the problem isn't the video but what it shows. Research shows that some consumers deliberately avoid information about meat production precisely so they won't have to change. This doesn't apply to those who find the images traumatic: for them there are other ways to be informed, such as accounts, reporting and data.
"Don't show me that at lunch. I'd rather not know. That's emotional terrorism."

No one is obliged to expose themselves to images that make them suffer.
Using shocking images is emotional manipulation, not argument.
So refusing to watch the videos is legitimate and says nothing about the moral question.

P1 and P2 are largely true: no one should be forced to watch violent scenes, and timing matters. P3 is partly true, but ignores that the images show facts. The problem lies in the conclusion: refusing to look doesn't change what happens, and those who pay for what happens have special reasons to know.
as a defense of the right not to be exposed to images. It fails when used to avoid knowing what one is funding.
"Vegans love posting slaughter videos to shock people."
"Do you want to ruin my meal?"
"Those videos are exceptions or staged." (which is B14)

Sometimes we don't want to look at something because it's sad. That's normal. But if we don't want to look because we know something wrong is happening, closing our eyes doesn't make it stop. It's like covering your ears when someone is asking for help.

If you can't bear to see what happens to the animals you eat, the problem isn't the video but what it shows. Refusing information so as not to feel the obligation is willful ignorance, and research shows that some consumers deliberately avoid information about meat production precisely so they won't have to change. If you find the images traumatic, you don't need to watch them: you can read accounts, reporting and data. What doesn't work is not wanting to know.
"If it's hard to watch how it's done, does it make sense to keep paying for it to be done?"
The argument can mean two things:
I don't want to see that during lunch
I'd rather not know how my food is produced
No: it's avoiding information relevant to one's own choice
Avoiding information so as not to feel obliged to act is a well-known strategy. It doesn't change the facts, only how they're perceived.
If seeing how it's done causes suffering, that indicates something morally relevant in what's seen. We don't feel this watching a bean harvest.
Calling them "emotional terrorism" suggests manipulation. But the emotion comes from what happens, and many scenes show legal, common practices (B10, B14).

A 2016 Dutch study with more than 3,200 participants identified a "strategically ignorant" group among consumers: it acknowledges that meat eaters bear responsibility for the problem, but avoids information about it. In the United States, in a survey of 1,000 Oklahoma residents, about a third admitted deliberately avoiding knowing how pigs are raised, and about a third chose to look at a blank screen rather than a photo of how pregnant sows are housed; the authors point to the wish to avoid guilt as one motive. Psychology also shows that being reminded of the link between meat and suffering leads people to attribute less mind to animals.

paragraph.text: No one has to watch everything that happens in the world. But when one directly funds something, knowing how it's done is part of a responsible choice.

paragraph.text: For people with trauma, anxiety, or who simply can't bear scenes of violence, refusing the images is legitimate. Written accounts, reporting, inspection reports and production data give the same information without the scenes. The refusal only becomes willful ignorance when it extends to every way of knowing.

The most serious version says the person already knows, broadly, that animals die to become food, and doesn't need to see the images to have that information. Refusing the images isn't refusing knowledge.

No one should be forced to watch violent images, and there are inappropriate times and ways to show them. For some people these images are genuinely traumatic, and there are other ways to be informed. Activists who use images carelessly can push people away, and the viewer's discomfort is real.
But discomfort is a signal, not an argument. If looking at something is unbearable, the question left is whether it makes sense to keep paying for it.
